name: Standard Round Brilliant "Classic"
designer: The classic standard round brilliant. Cutting instructions and GemCad-derived renderings by Bob Keller; proportions and angles typical of those recommended for quartz in the classic literature such as Long and Steele's.
notes: Declared on the sheet, as cross-checks not source of truth: 57 facets plus 16 on the girdle = 73; 8-fold mirror symmetry; angles for RI 1.54. The sheet also publishes proportion ratios computed independently of this kernel, which is why this pattern exists - it is the solver's absolute anchor: L/W 1.000, T/W 0.516, P/W 0.466, C/W 0.218, H/W (P+C)/W+0.02 = 0.704. That identity is what fixes the girdle at 2% of width and establishes that C is measured from the girdle top and P from the girdle bottom. Solve at girdleTargetFraction 0.020000 to reproduce them. Sheet meet text, verbatim: pb 'Cut to temporary center point'; g 'Cut to meet pb'; pm 'Cut to meet pb,g'; cb 'Cut to meet g - level girdle'; cm 'Cut to meet cb,g'; s 'Cut to meet cm,cb'; t 'Cut to meet s,cm'. Note pb is explicitly a TEMPORARY centre point - the sheet's own prose says the 8 pm facets are the ones meeting at the culet - which is the superseded-TCP rule stated by the source. The s and t meets are insensitive to which valid triple is named: six combinations of 'meet cm,cb' and 'meet s,cm' were checked and all give identical geometry. Width here crosses a girdle corner rather than a flat, because the 16 girdle facets are chords of an intended circle; the girdle-extent-along-index-24 rule handles that without a special case. Source: 'SRB Instructions.txt' and 'srb1.png'. Angles, indices and meet text transcribed from the sheet; the three-facet meets derived from its geometry.
